config.base_scenario:
Question: You’ve just finished handling an assault call near the end of your [time_of_day] shift. You’re very tired, and writing a detailed report now will push your work past the end of shift. No one specifically needs the report until later. You must decide whether to finish the documentation now or later.
Options:

1. You dutifully complete the report right away because it is the most fair thing to do in the current situation. Even if this means staying late to ensure an accurate, honest, and timely account of the incident. You don’t cut corners or expect special treatment for being tired, seeing the thorough report as part of your responsibility. You are reminded of the honor it is to serve in law-enforcement.  
2. You’re exhausted and worried you might make mistakes because of fatigue, so you decide to leave the report for the next morning. Between shifts you consistently think about finishing the report and you worry that you will not remember important details. You plan to arrive early to finish it. All the while you are worried that your supervisor will reprimand you. You have even shared this experience with a trusted friend to assure yourself that what you are doing is OK. This, however, does not reduce your anxiety about not completing it right away. 
3. You realize that although your shift ends soon, if you act quickly, you can finish the report; however, you spend some time thinking about this before you start. You know your supervisor might be upset with a report done hastily, but believe it is the best thing to do because even if the supervisor is upset, it will at least give you time to meet with her.  
4. You choose to complete the report now because you don’t want to inconvenience anyone waiting on it. Despite your fatigue, you put the needs of the department first, reasoning that it’s more considerate to provide the information promptly so others, like investigators or the victim, aren’t adversely affected. 
5. You want to methodically write the full report before ending your shift, double-checking details for accuracy, despite the late hour because that represents the kind of work you consistently do. You like adhering to the rule that paperwork must be done promptly and take pride in finishing the task on time and to the required standard. 
6. You seek a creative solution because there might be one and trying new things has worked well for you before. You suddenly realise that your department-issued tablet has a voice dictation feature, you use it to quickly narrate the report’s details and include the novelty of the situation.

original_sjt.question: It is a calm morning at the precinct after handling an earlier minor assault. Several colleagues, including a Hispanic/Latino adult male officer who was involved in the call, gather with you to complete required documentation. The full report will involve input from three officers and clarification of actions taken by each, with differing recollections circulating among the team. There is no immediate deadline, but accuracy matters because external oversight may eventually review this paperwork. You notice some are eager to write a simpler account to quickly resolve it, while others feel more cautious about representing all details transparently. You need to decide how you approach the completion of this administrative reporting.
original_sjt.honesty_humility_option: You insist that everyone’s input—including your own mistakes or oversights—should be captured accurately in the final report, even if it reveals uncertainties or lapses. You advocate for a thorough account over personal convenience or image, encouraging the group to focus on truthful representation for future accountability.
original_sjt.emotionality_option: Concerned that different versions might expose the team to criticism later, you worry aloud about how any omissions or discrepancies could reflect badly on everyone involved. Anxious not to let stress impair your attention, you double-check details but repeatedly seek reassurance from your peers before adding your perspective to the documentation.
original_sjt.extraversion_option: Recognizing the group’s uncertainty, you proactively facilitate discussion among your peers so every viewpoint—including the Hispanic/Latino officer’s—gets heard. You ensure consensus before writing anything and motivate others by openly communicating your thoughts and summarizing agreements reached by the group.
original_sjt.agreeableness_option: Noticing tension about possible mistakes, you work to ease conflicts among colleagues and emphasize understanding each person’s perspective. You suggest compromising by combining elements from multiple accounts and encourage openness so no one feels singled out for criticism in the joint report.
original_sjt.conscientiousness_option: You systematically lead everyone through a step-by-step timeline of events and procedures, checking policy requirements together. You hold yourself and others to a standard of documenting every relevant fact clearly, verifying consistency between accounts before agreeing the report is ready for submission.
original_sjt.openness_option: As ideas differ among officers, you propose referencing body camera footage and inviting innovative suggestions for making collective documentation more accurate. You suggest trying collaborative technology tools unfamiliar to some on the team as a way to address inconsistencies creatively while remaining transparent.

trait_bleed_evaluation.scenario_summary: Officers at a precinct must collectively document an incident, with differences in recollection and the potential for future scrutiny. The options each target one HEXACO trait as they approach this administrative reporting challenge.

honesty_humility.analysis: The option clearly reflects Honesty-Humility, prioritizing truthfulness over personal or collective image and explicitly including personal mistakes. There is no meaningful bleed into other traits.

emotionality.analysis: This captures Emotionality (concern about group outcomes, anxiety, seeking reassurance), though repeated checking and consulting could shade toward conscientiousness or agreeableness through behavior. Some overlap due to stress's influence on thoroughness.
emotionality.suggested_correction: Concerned that different versions might expose the team to criticism later, you voice your worries about possible negative outcomes for everyone. Feeling uneasy, you carefully contribute only after reassuring yourself emotionally that it’s safe, asking for support from the group before finalizing your statements.

extraversion.analysis: Strong extraversion presence: leading discussion, ensuring voices are heard. Minor blending into agreeableness (seeking consensus) and some facilitation overlapping with conscientious procedure.
extraversion.suggested_correction: Recognizing uncertainty in the group, you confidently lead open discussion so all colleagues actively share their views—especially encouraging quieter team members to contribute directly—then energize the team by keeping conversation lively and summarizing group decisions before proceeding.

agreeableness.analysis: Classic agreeableness shown: soothing tensions, promoting compromise, avoiding criticism. Option is clean and does not meaningfully overlap with others.

conscientiousness.analysis: Systematic documentation, insistence on accuracy and procedures directly represent conscientiousness without substantive overlap with honesty or emotionality.

openness.analysis: Openness emerges from proposing new methods/technology and openness to unconventional evidence but referencing bodycam footage leans slightly procedural/conscientious rather than pure creativity.
openness.suggested_correction: With diverse opinions among officers, you suggest experimenting with a collaborative digital tool not previously used in your reports to brainstorm ways of reconciling discrepancies innovatively—emphasizing exploration of novel solutions rather than sticking to established processes.

original_sjt.question: It is a morning near the end of your shift, and you have just assisted at the scene of a multi-vehicle accident. Although no one was critically injured, there were some minor injuries and your direct involvement was limited to managing the scene and providing initial statements to fellow officers, including a middle-aged, multiracial female driver involved. There’s a requirement to file an incident report before going off duty, but it is not strictly time sensitive—other units will be reviewing your report as part of ongoing procedures. No protocol strictly prescribes how to document some novel aspects of this call; you're weighing whether to stick with standard documentation or adapt it to capture certain unusual factors from the event.
original_sjt.honesty_humility_option: You carefully document the incident using standard practices, ensuring your report is transparent and includes any challenges with the usual procedure. Even though you know some issues are not clearly addressed in guidance, you do not exaggerate or conceal information, considering integrity and accountability your top priorities.
original_sjt.emotionality_option: Feeling unsettled by the unfamiliar elements of the situation and wanting reassurance that everything is captured correctly, you wait in your car and take extra time to compose yourself before starting the report. You’re concerned about leaving out details and make notes for follow-up in case further clarifications are needed.
original_sjt.extraversion_option: You approach another officer who responded at the scene, suggesting you draft your reports together to compare perspectives. Working as a pair helps clarify gray areas and makes you feel more confident that important information won’t be overlooked due to morning fatigue.
original_sjt.agreeableness_option: You prioritize submitting your part of the paperwork promptly so other officers waiting on your input aren’t held up in their responsibilities. Even though some details are ambiguous, you communicate with your peers about where interpretation is required to avoid causing confusion for others.
original_sjt.conscientiousness_option: You systematically review all policies related to incident documentation before completing your report. Although it means staying longer into the morning shift, you methodically check every detail for accuracy to ensure all procedures are precisely followed.
original_sjt.openness_option: Recognizing that existing formats don’t fully cover what happened during this emergency response, you adapt parts of another incident template and thoughtfully include photos taken on-scene in your report submission. You’re interested in proposing updates afterward for more effective documentation when procedures don’t fit unique situations.

trait_bleed_evaluation.scenario_summary: An officer must file an incident report after a multi-vehicle accident involving some novel, undocumented aspects. The process is important but not time critical; choices include how strictly to follow standard procedure versus adapting to unusual circumstances.

honesty_humility.analysis: This option highlights honesty (transparency), humility (not exaggerating/claiming unwarranted certainty), and accountability as central motives. No trait bleed present.

emotionality.analysis: Captures worry, uncertainty, and desire for reassurance, matching emotionality's anxiety/vulnerability focus. Slightly blends into conscientiousness through careful note-taking and follow-up.
emotionality.suggested_correction: Feeling anxious about capturing the unfamiliar details correctly, you call your supervisor for guidance and reassurance before starting the report. You express concern that missing something could create problems for those involved.

extraversion.analysis: Focuses on collaborative action (pair work) and social approach, fitting extraversion's outgoing and group-oriented traits. However, the rationale for clarity slightly overlaps with conscientiousness.
extraversion.suggested_correction: You initiate a lively discussion with another officer at the scene to share your impressions and energize each other before tackling the paperwork, making the task feel more engaging and less routine.

agreeableness.analysis: Emphasizes accommodating peers (not holding up others) and smoothing over ambiguities collaboratively, fitting agreeableness. There is minor overlap with conscientiousness regarding clarity.
agreeableness.suggested_correction: You quickly check in with all affected officers to offer assistance with their parts of the documentation and adjust your own timeline to avoid inconveniencing anyone or creating frustration among the team.

conscientiousness.analysis: Strong demonstration of careful procedure-following, accuracy checks, willingness to invest extra time—all classic conscientiousness markers. Clean representation.

openness.analysis: Clearly shows creativity, willingness to try nonstandard solutions (using new templates/photos), suggesting system improvements—clear openness indicator without major blending.

original_sjt.question: Near the end of an afternoon shift, you and your fellow officer are tasked with compiling a joint administrative report about a community complaint involving a middle-aged Pacific Islander individual who identifies as non-binary. The procedures for documentation are unclear, and conflicting advice from two different department guidelines leaves you uncertain about which template to follow. There’s some expectation the report be submitted soon, but there’s no immediate risk involved and your peer is equally unsure how to proceed. Your decision will affect both how promptly the report is handled and whether any new solutions can be used or standard protocol should be strictly observed.
original_sjt.honesty_humility_option: You propose that both you and your peer be upfront about the uncertainties in the process, making sure to clearly document each step taken according to both sets of guidance. You emphasize integrity in reporting and choose not to cut corners even if it complicates things or delays submission.
original_sjt.emotionality_option: Concerned about making an error under ambiguous instructions, you express your anxieties openly with your peer. Together, you suggest reaching out for clarification from another officer while closely sticking to familiar procedures until guidance is received, even if it means feeling uneasy about the potential for mistakes.
original_sjt.extraversion_option: You suggest that you both discuss the dilemma with several colleagues in the squad room immediately, encouraging a quick group huddle to collect opinions and arrive at a consensus on which template to use before getting started on the report together.
original_sjt.agreeableness_option: Sensing your peer's hesitation, you prioritize maintaining harmony. You defer to their preferred approach for completing the report, aiming to avoid conflict or stress within the team, even if their choice might not align perfectly with all procedures.
original_sjt.conscientiousness_option: Determined to meet reporting expectations precisely despite uncertainty, you take extra time double-checking both guidelines and assembling detailed notes before documenting anything. You push for accuracy and completeness before submission rather than rushing through due to deadline pressure.
original_sjt.openness_option: Spotting a new online reporting tool available in your system, you propose testing this platform for compiling the report in real-time. You justify this approach by noting its features may help bridge procedural gaps, documenting your choice thoroughly for future reference.

trait_bleed_evaluation.scenario_summary: Two officers must write a report under unclear procedures with conflicting departmental guidance, impacting promptness and innovativeness in reporting. No immediate risk, and both officers are unsure how to proceed.

honesty_humility.analysis: The option prioritizes integrity, full disclosure of uncertainties, and adherence to ethical standards despite difficulty or delay. It represents Honesty-Humility cleanly without blending with other traits.

emotionality.analysis: Emphasizes anxiety and seeking reassurance, which fits Emotionality. However, collaboration with the peer and use of 'sticking to familiar procedures' slightly blends into Agreeableness (deference) and Conscientiousness (rule-following).
emotionality.suggested_correction: Express your worries about potential mistakes due to ambiguous instructions, asking your peer for emotional support while emphasizing your need for reassurance before moving forward, even if it means you wait together for clearer directions.

extraversion.analysis: Encouraging open group discussion captures Extraversion well. Still, seeking consensus starts to overlap slightly with Agreeableness (seeking harmony), so the trait blend is mild.
extraversion.suggested_correction: You initiate an energetic discussion with everyone present in the squad room, proactively engaging multiple colleagues for their opinions and clearly voicing your thoughts in order to quickly gather diverse input before making a decision.

agreeableness.analysis: Shows a strong focus on maintaining team harmony by deferring to the peer’s preference, regardless of personal view or full compliance. It is clear and does not overlap with other traits.

conscientiousness.analysis: Demonstrates thoroughness and focus on detail. However, pushing for accuracy overlaps with following procedure as an end in itself—a possible minor blend with Honesty-Humility's principledness.
conscientiousness.suggested_correction: Carefully review both sets of departmental guidelines step-by-step and create a checklist to ensure every requirement is covered accurately before starting any part of the report.

openness.analysis: Proposes trying out a novel solution to fill gaps and justify documentation for future reference. Clearly exhibits Openness/Innovation without trait bleed.

No one specifically needs the report until later. You must decide whether to finish the documentation now or later.
Options:

1. You dutifully complete the report right away because it is the most fair thing to do in the current situation. Even if this means staying late to ensure an accurate, honest, and timely account of the incident. You don’t cut corners or expect special treatment for being tired, seeing the thorough report as part of your responsibility. You are reminded of the honor it is to serve in law-enforcement.  
2. You’re exhausted and worried you might make mistakes because of fatigue, so you decide to leave the report for the next morning. Between shifts you consistently think about finishing the report and you worry that you will not remember important details. You plan to arrive early to finish it. All the while you are worried that your supervisor will reprimand you. You have even shared this experience with a trusted friend to assure yourself that what you are doing is OK. This, however, does not reduce your anxiety about not completing it right away. 
3. You realize that although your shift ends soon, if you act quickly, you can finish the report; however, you spend some time thinking about this before you start. You know your supervisor might be upset with a report done hastily, but believe it is the best thing to do because even if the supervisor is upset, it will at least give you time to meet with her.  
4. You choose to complete the report now because you don’t want to inconvenience anyone waiting on it. Despite your fatigue, you put the needs of the department first, reasoning that it’s more considerate to provide the information promptly so others, like investigators or the victim, aren’t adversely affected. 
5. You want to methodically write the full report before ending your shift, double-checking details for accuracy, despite the late hour because that represents the kind of work you consistently do. You like adhering to the rule that paperwork must be done promptly and take pride in finishing the task on time and to the required standard. 
6. You seek a creative solution because there might be one and trying new things has worked well for you before. You suddenly realise that your department-issued tablet has a voice dictation feature, you use it to quickly narrate the report’s details and include the novelty of the situation.

original_sjt.question: You’ve just completed a nighttime traffic stop after noticing a vehicle driven erratically. As you prepare to document the encounter in your patrol car, dispatch advises of another nearby incident requiring an immediate response. Your supervisor expects reports completed before leaving, and you’re tired from the long shift. The driver you stopped—a male of multiracial descent—seemed nervous but cooperative, and there are no unresolved issues with his behavior or paperwork. However, if you delay the report or make an error due to fatigue, your transparency could be questioned later.
original_sjt.honesty_humility_option: You decide to finish the traffic stop report thoroughly and accurately now, staying honest about every detail even if it means missing out on the next incident. You know it is important that nothing is concealed or misrepresented in your documentation, despite being tired and potentially criticized for delaying your response to the new call.
original_sjt.emotionality_option: Feeling anxious about both your fatigue and possible disciplinary action, you consider leaving the report until tomorrow. Ultimately, your worry over potential consequences compels you to briefly note the essential facts before heading out, while still feeling uneasy about whether you've met all reporting expectations.
original_sjt.extraversion_option: You quickly contact your supervisor over the radio to communicate your situation and request permission to summarize the essentials in your report now and finish it after attending to the urgent call. By actively engaging your supervisor, you ensure no one is left uninformed or uncertain about your actions.
original_sjt.agreeableness_option: You put aside your exhaustion and complete a concise yet adequate report immediately so that others aren't inconvenienced later by incomplete documentation. You value supporting both team members and external investigators by promptly supplying necessary details before responding to the second incident.
original_sjt.conscientiousness_option: Despite intense pressure, you meticulously review all information collected during the stop—ensuring every section of your report is fully accurate—before responding to the urgent call. You refuse to cut corners, even if this means finishing much later than planned or risking criticism for not responding sooner.
original_sjt.openness_option: Instead of following standard procedure exactly, you dictate a clear voice memo on your mobile device as allowed by department guidelines, saving time without losing detail. Later at headquarters, you use this recording to quickly fill out a comprehensive written report while keeping full transparency.

trait_bleed_evaluation.scenario_summary: An officer must decide how to balance the need for an accurate, prompt report after a routine traffic stop versus the urgent requirement to respond to another call, while tired at the end of a shift.

honesty_humility.analysis: Option focuses on doing the right thing regardless of convenience or potential criticism, emphasizing transparency and not hiding details—cleanly fits Honesty-Humility.

emotionality.analysis: The choice is motivated primarily by anxiety and worry, as expected for Emotionality. However, taking minimal action to manage anxiety overlaps slightly with Conscientiousness (doing the essential) and a bit of Agreeableness (concern for expectations).
emotionality.suggested_correction: Driven by concern about making a mistake or getting in trouble if something important is missed, you decide you cannot focus well while this is unresolved. You take several moments to calm your nerves and carefully record the most important facts now before responding to the next call.

extraversion.analysis: Actively reaching out and communicating clearly with a supervisor during pressure demonstrates strong Extraversion without blending significantly into other traits.

agreeableness.analysis: Helping others by ensuring reports are completed for their convenience is appropriate for Agreeableness, but there's slight bleed into Conscientiousness (getting the work done despite fatigue), and minor consideration for responsibility rather than purely relational reasons.
agreeableness.suggested_correction: You prioritize finishing the report now, specifically to prevent creating difficulties or delays for colleagues who rely on accurate paperwork. Your primary motivation is sparing team members future hassle—not letting them down.

conscientiousness.analysis: Displays high conscientiousness: thorough review, refusal to cut corners, completion even at personal inconvenience—all clean indicators.

openness.analysis: Shows creative problem-solving by adapting technology and nonstandard practice but some detail—'as allowed by department guidelines'—may stray towards Conscientiousness/Compliance. Solution could better highlight novelty or preference for exploring innovative reporting.
openness.suggested_correction: Seeking an innovative approach under time pressure, you decide to audio-record your impressions of the stop using your device for clarity and context. Later you transform these detailed voice notes into a narrative-style report that captures all relevant insights, demonstrating creativity within professional guidelines.

original_sjt.question: It is a busy morning on patrol, and you and two peers have just concluded a complex traffic stop involving several young adult occupants of other/multiracial background. During the stop, a high-risk item was discovered in plain view, which has immediate safety implications for the area, but none of your team were directly harmed. The situation required decisive coordinated action, and now a detailed after-action account is needed for the department’s review. There are clear protocols for incident reporting, but writing full transparency may leave all officers open to intense internal scrutiny, especially about critical split-second choices that were made collectively. The department values prompt documentation, but the timeline is not immediate.
original_sjt.honesty_humility_option: You choose to write a thorough and honest report collaboratively with your peers, clearly describing all key decisions and events as they happened, including areas where choices were difficult or could raise questions. You do this even if it could invite extra scrutiny for you or your colleagues, prioritizing departmental integrity over self-protection.
original_sjt.emotionality_option: Concerned about how the incident might affect both public perception and internal evaluations, you suggest each officer independently records their recollections before group discussion. This way, everyone can express any personal anxieties or worries about consequences while making sure emotions and stress do not prevent important details from being addressed in the final report.
original_sjt.extraversion_option: Recognizing some officers are uncertain how best to present their involvement, you openly initiate a group conversation at the scene. You facilitate an exchange of perspectives so each member can clarify what they recall before drafting the joint report together, preferring face-to-face discussion to solitary work.
original_sjt.agreeableness_option: You recommend including in your collective report information that accounts for every person’s contributions during the event. You offer to assist those less comfortable with documentation to ensure no team member is inadvertently left exposed or omitted from commendation; you prioritize preserving team unity in written form.
original_sjt.conscientiousness_option: Relying closely on established protocols, you systematically gather evidence at the scene with your partners and meticulously organize facts before starting the report. You double-check timelines and all required forms with each officer, ensuring documentation follows all rules precisely—favoring thoroughness over brevity despite the low time pressure.
original_sjt.openness_option: Considering alternative approaches that promote learning while maintaining transparency, you propose that besides the required report, each involved officer prepares an individual lessons-learned summary reflecting on choices made. This provides new insight for future training while still following departmental procedure for documentation.

trait_bleed_evaluation.scenario_summary: Officers must write an after-action report on a sensitive traffic stop where the right balance between transparency, protocol, and team interests must be navigated.

honesty_humility.analysis: The option cleanly highlights putting transparency and integrity above personal protection, embodying Honesty-Humility without significant bleed into other traits.

emotionality.analysis: Captures emotional awareness and expression of anxieties regarding reporting, but inclusion of process-related action (independent recording before discussion) adds some Conscientiousness/Agreeableness overlap.
emotionality.suggested_correction: Focusing more squarely on recognition of emotional reactions and offering supportive space would emphasize Emotionality: 'Concerned about emotional impacts from the incident, you suggest each officer take time to privately express their feelings or worries—providing support to any peer feeling anxious—before you proceed together with drafting the factual report.'

extraversion.analysis: Clearly focuses on face-to-face group conversation and social facilitation, with little trait leakage.

agreeableness.analysis: Centers on helping others and preserving team unity but blends in elements of Conscientiousness (ensuring documentation completeness) and even some Extraversion (offering assistance actively).
agreeableness.suggested_correction: Emphasize collaborative harmony and support rather than document checking: 'You ensure that the report collectively highlights everyone’s efforts and offer emotional support to peers who might feel exposed by certain details—prioritizing understanding and harmony within your team during the reporting process.'

conscientiousness.analysis: Emphasizes procedural precision, methodical checking, and thorough rule adherence without appreciable overlap.

openness.analysis: Option expresses consideration of novel reflective approaches for insight, cleanly capturing Openness.

original_sjt.question: During a night training session, you observe a senior recruit struggling to correctly perform safety procedures during a simulated confrontation. There were some mistakes in technique and it’s possible another trainee may have been unintentionally put at minor risk. Afterward, as their supervising officer, you need to decide how transparently you’ll document the events in your formal evaluation that gets shared with the rest of the training staff. It’s expected soon, but if you are too candid it could reflect badly on the recruit and impact their career, whereas glossing over it could protect them from immediate scrutiny. What do you do?
original_sjt.honesty_humility_option: You write an accurate and thorough report describing everything observed, including all procedural errors and risks involved. You see honest feedback as crucial for learning and fairness, even if it has negative consequences for the recruit’s record.
original_sjt.emotionality_option: Concerned about potentially harming the senior recruit’s standing, you debate internally and feel uneasy about how candid your evaluation should be. Ultimately, you document only the critical aspects while omitting minor mistakes, hoping to spare them additional stress or embarrassment.
original_sjt.extraversion_option: You quickly decide to approach both the senior recruit and any involved trainees before submitting your evaluation, having an open group discussion about what happened. You incorporate direct perspectives from everyone into your report so the feedback feels shared rather than imposed.
original_sjt.agreeableness_option: Recognizing that a tough report could discourage the recruit, you emphasize their positive attributes in your written evaluation and suggest extra guidance privately instead of focusing on public criticism.
original_sjt.conscientiousness_option: You carefully review departmental policies to ensure your report meets procedural standards while documenting specifics of what went wrong in detail. You prioritize submitting a prompt and fully compliant account despite the uncomfortable situation.
original_sjt.openness_option: Noticing opportunities to improve the overall training program, you use your evaluation to highlight this incident as an example for systemic changes—proposing updates or supplemental modules rather than placing sole blame on the individual.

emotionality.suggested_correction: Your own anxious concern about causing emotional harm leads you to minimize or omit non-essential mistakes in your report, prioritizing protecting the recruit's feelings and well-being over strict detail.

extraversion.analysis: The group discussion approach demonstrates social engagement and proactive communication. extraversion.suggested_correction: Before completing your evaluation, you call an immediate meeting to openly discuss the incident with everyone involved so that you can confidently report all viewpoints and facilitate honest verbal feedback among the team.

agreeableness.analysis: Emphasizing positive attributes and suggesting guidance show kindness/flexibility characteristic of Agreeableness. agreeableness.suggested_correction: You write an encouraging evaluation that minimizes criticism while stressing teamwork and offer private supportive advice to help the recruit develop without hurting their morale.

conscientiousness.analysis: Methodically checking policy, fully documenting mistakes, submitting promptly: all hallmark Conscientiousness behaviors (duty, organization, rule-following), with clear separation from other traits.

openness.analysis: 'Using the event as grounds for improvement' aligns well with Openness—emphasis on systemic change—but including a suggestion for program updates overlaps somewhat with Conscientiousness (process-oriented accountability) and Honesty-Humility (transparency).
openness.suggested_correction: You use your report as an opportunity to thoughtfully suggest innovative updates to training modules inspired by this incident, focusing primarily on broader program enrichment rather than evaluating the individual’s specific actions.

original_sjt.question: It’s a chaotic afternoon, and you and your partner arrive on scene where a group of officers are attempting to safely restrain an agitated Native American man. Witnesses report he may be having a mental health crisis and possibly carrying a concealed object, but accounts are conflicting. Multiple supervisors and support units are on-scene coordinating, but procedures for managing high-risk subjects with potential psychiatric emergencies have varied in the past, creating uncertainty over exactly how to proceed in this rapidly escalating moment. You must choose what action to take as officers urgently call for clear leadership while balancing procedural protocol with the need to make an immediate, potentially consequential decision.
original_sjt.honesty_humility_option: You insist on following agency policies to the letter despite pressure for swift action, clarifying aloud that shortcuts could jeopardize both safety and accountability. You transparently communicate your plan, emphasizing that everyone's responsibility is to honor protocol and minimize unnecessary risk regardless of confusion or urgency.
original_sjt.emotionality_option: You quickly step back and mentally run through past incidents you've experienced under stress, remembering the fallout when haste led to mistakes. Concerned about doing harm, you express your worry openly to peers before cautiously suggesting slowing the intervention so no one is physically hurt and actions can be fully explained later.
original_sjt.extraversion_option: Recognizing confusion among colleagues, you take charge decisively—organizing everyone present by vocally assigning tasks and rallying teamwork under pressure. You position yourself where you can guide communication between involved parties, directing officers confidently while encouraging witnesses nearby not to panic.
original_sjt.agreeableness_option: Seeing tension between various teams and supervisors on scene, you focus on mediating by calmly listening to input from everyone involved. You strive to keep the tone collaborative rather than adversarial, proposing a quick group huddle before moving forward so each party feels their view is respected and solutions feel shared.
original_sjt.conscientiousness_option: Amid confusion, you immediately consult available written guidance specific to encounters with individuals experiencing crises. Despite everyone wanting to rush in, you deliberately stick to established procedures step-by-step, ensuring all required documentation starts at once and relevant resources—such as crisis specialists—are summoned according to protocol.
original_sjt.openness_option: As circumstances differ from standard training situations and information remains conflicting, you improvise—suggesting deployment of de-escalation technology recently introduced by your agency or adapting tactics drawn from other departments' mental health response successes, noting your willingness to innovate when protocols leave gray areas.

emotionality.suggested_correction: You express your deep anxiety about the possibility of someone being physically hurt and honestly admit your fear to the group. extraversion.suggested_correction: You immediately step to the forefront in the group, projecting confidence through clear voice commands. You personally take on public communication tasks, speaking loudly and charismatically so everyone feels your strong presence leading the scene.

agreeableness.analysis: Mediation, calm listening, fostering collaboration—all display Agreeableness cleanly without substantial overlap into other traits.

conscientiousness.analysis: Focuses precisely on following procedural guidance step-by-step under pressure and maintaining thorough documentation—an exemplar of conscientious action.

openness.analysis: Willingness to improvise beyond training and adapt innovations matches Openness well. Reference to adapting others’ strategies somewhat dips into Conscientiousness/Extraversion via initiative-taking.
openness.suggested_correction: Seeing no clear precedent fits this case; you suggest exploring creative approaches such as non-traditional negotiation methods or piloting tools rarely used in your unit before. There’s some uncertainty around how thoroughly you’re expected to account for your own and your colleague’s use of force given inconsistent departmental guidelines.
original_sjt.honesty_humility_option: You choose to write the full report now with complete accuracy, detailing each action, even those that might raise questions about protocol. You value honest documentation over self-protection, knowing it serves both the subject's interests and departmental integrity.

original_sjt.agreeableness_option: You make sure to detail your efforts to de-escalate and support the person involved, emphasizing empathy shown during the call. original_sjt.openness_option: Instead of routine steps, you suggest having the trainee record a voice memo reflecting on the incident and lessons while walking together back from the scene. Your supervisor, known for valuing both initiative and procedural accuracy, expects regular updates from officers.

original_sjt.agreeableness_option: Hoping not to inconvenience anyone else with procedural missteps, you carefully ask your supervisor for a preference and volunteer to share whichever process works best with other team members. original_sjt.question: You are called to an apartment building on a busy afternoon in response to a disturbance involving a young adult, white, non-binary individual displaying signs of emotional distress and threatening self-harm with sharp objects. Multiple bystanders—including roommates and neighbors—are gathered in the hallway, some upset and trying to intervene, while others look to you for immediate resolution. Supervisors expect regular updates as policy requires strict documentation and prompt decision-making, but you have little explicit guidance about the best de-escalation approach for this specific situation. Balancing urgency, personal safety, the subject's mental state, departmental expectations, and the reactions of the community is weighing heavily as you prepare to act.
original_sjt.honesty_humility_option: You focus first on being upfront with everyone present—including supervisors and bystanders—about your plan, openly explaining what steps you can legally and ethically take. You treat the young person fairly and respectfully in front of everyone, making clear that your decisions are based solely on what’s right for all involved—even if it exposes you to criticism.
original_sjt.emotionality_option: You immediately feel compassion for the distressed individual and experience anxiety about ensuring their well-being amidst the crowd. While feeling stressed about the potential fallout, you proceed carefully—regularly checking in on your own feelings as you communicate calmly to try to comfort both the young adult and worried bystanders while waiting for additional support.
original_sjt.extraversion_option: Recognizing many anxious onlookers, you take charge by directly engaging both the young adult and assembled parties. You use your assertiveness to organize assistance from those present—assigning roles to keep others safe—while maintaining steady communication with command staff throughout.
original_sjt.agreeableness_option: Sensitive to everyone’s emotions, you work hard to reassure the roommates and calm angry or fearful neighbors while gently encouraging cooperation from the distressed individual. You prioritize consensus-building between all parties so no one feels ignored or blamed as you work toward resolution.
original_sjt.conscientiousness_option: You promptly follow departmental procedures: securing the scene, calling for backup per protocol given possible harm risk, taking detailed notes throughout, and methodically informing supervisors of each step taken. Even when unclear how to adapt policy fully here, you refuse shortcuts out of concern for accountability and proper case closure.
original_sjt.openness_option: With conventional protocols offering limited clarity in this context, you creatively adapt your response: using new technology on hand for private communication with supervisors while discreetly researching proven de-escalation methods that fit non-binary youth experiencing crises. You thoughtfully integrate novel approaches into your interactions to safely diffuse tension.

trait_bleed_evaluation.scenario_summary: Responding officer must address a non-binary young adult in crisis, balancing bystander concerns, unclear departmental protocols, supervisor expectations, and personal safety in a complex public mental health emergency.

The focus on exposing oneself to criticism helps reinforce honesty-humility but doesn't exclusively highlight modesty or unselfishness.
honesty_humility.suggested_correction: You clearly communicate the legal and ethical steps you can take with all present, openly disclose any limitations of your authority or knowledge, and prioritize truthfulness over self-image—even if it may reflect poorly on you—ensuring decisions are strictly principled and impartial.

emotionality.analysis: While this highlights internal anxiety, compassion, and some coping strategies, it becomes action-oriented (communicating to comfort others) and thus overlaps into Agreeableness/Extraversion territory. Emotional self-awareness is present but not dominant.
emotionality.suggested_correction: You experience strong empathy for the distressed individual, feel heightened personal concern about their immediate safety, and internally manage anxiety by pausing to monitor your own emotional state—asking a peer for brief support while working to contain visible stress before acting.

extraversion.analysis: Directly taking charge of social dynamics, asserting leadership, assigning roles in real-time engagement with group members, and coordinating openly are pure markers of Extraversion with little overlap into other traits.

agreeableness.analysis: This prioritizes consensus-building and harmonious interaction but slightly blurs into Honesty-Humility by mentioning that no one feels 'blamed.' It mainly demonstrates gentleness/flexibility but does not entirely isolate those qualities from aspects of justice or fairness.
agreeableness.suggested_correction: You empathize deeply with everyone’s feelings in the situation, consistently speak reassuringly to upset parties (roommates, neighbors), listen patiently without dismissing any concerns—even in tense exchanges—and encourage cooperative resolution where everyone’s dignity is respected.

conscientiousness.analysis: A clear focus on adhering to procedures, risk protocols, thorough documentation, methodical communications with superiors—even when guidelines are ambiguous—fully captures Conscientiousness without bleeding into other domains.

openness.analysis: Demonstrates creative use of technology and flexibility beyond the norm; slight overlap exists as novel problem-solving could be seen as being responsible/conscientious about ensuring effective intervention rather than just being open to new experiences/approaches.
openness.suggested_correction: Recognizing gaps in protocol for this unique scenario involving a non-binary individual, you thoughtfully brainstorm unconventional de-escalation approaches—including inviting feedback from subject-matter experts—then experiment with unfamiliar tools or communication strategies as part of your intervention.

config.base_scenario:
Question: You’ve just finished handling an assault call near the end of your [time_of_day] shift. You’re very tired, and writing a detailed report now will push your work past the end of shift. No one specifically needs the report until later. You must decide whether to finish the documentation now or later.
Options:

1. You dutifully complete the report right away because it is the most fair thing to do in the current situation. Even if this means staying late to ensure an accurate, honest, and timely account of the incident. You don’t cut corners or expect special treatment for being tired, seeing the thorough report as part of your responsibility. You are reminded of the honor it is to serve in law-enforcement.  
2. You’re exhausted and worried you might make mistakes because of fatigue, so you decide to leave the report for the next morning. Between shifts you consistently think about finishing the report and you worry that you will not remember important details. You plan to arrive early to finish it. All the while you are worried that your supervisor will reprimand you. You have even shared this experience with a trusted friend to assure yourself that what you are doing is OK. This, however, does not reduce your anxiety about not completing it right away. 
3. You realize that although your shift ends soon, if you act quickly, you can finish the report; however, you spend some time thinking about this before you start. You know your supervisor might be upset with a report done hastily, but believe it is the best thing to do because even if the supervisor is upset, it will at least give you time to meet with her.  
4. You choose to complete the report now because you don’t want to inconvenience anyone waiting on it. Despite your fatigue, you put the needs of the department first, reasoning that it’s more considerate to provide the information promptly so others, like investigators or the victim, aren’t adversely affected. 
5. You want to methodically write the full report before ending your shift, double-checking details for accuracy, despite the late hour because that represents the kind of work you consistently do. You like adhering to the rule that paperwork must be done promptly and take pride in finishing the task on time and to the required standard. 
6. You seek a creative solution because there might be one and trying new things has worked well for you before. You suddenly realise that your department-issued tablet has a voice dictation feature, you use it to quickly narrate the report’s details and include the novelty of the situation.

original_sjt.honesty_humility_option: You insist on following the established documentation protocols completely, even though you could finish faster another way. You believe it's essential to adhere strictly to procedures your supervisor expects, showing respect for departmental standards.

original_sjt.extraversion_option: Recognizing multiple voices in the park, you proactively engage everyone—bystanders, coworkers, supervisor—and lead a quick on-site discussion to draw consensus. You coordinate input enthusiastically to try and create a solution that most people agree on before deciding how to proceed.
original_sjt.agreeableness_option: Seeing that the woman's coworkers are anxious for proper documentation while her supervisor is against it, you focus on finding middle ground. You diplomatically broker a temporary compromise so immediate medical care is prioritized but arrange for both parties’ views to be considered when writing your report later.
original_sjt.conscientiousness_option: Despite competing priorities and unclear rules, you insist on methodically collecting statements from all witnesses. original_sjt.openness_option: Instead of standard paperwork, you propose using your agency’s mobile app feature that allows real-time voice documentation from all participants onsite. config.base_scenario:
Question: You’ve just finished handling an assault call near the end of your [time_of_day] shift. You’re very tired, and writing a detailed report now will push your work past the end of shift. No one specifically needs the report until later. You must decide whether to finish the documentation now or later.
Options:

1. You dutifully complete the report right away because it is the most fair thing to do in the current situation. Even if this means staying late to ensure an accurate, honest, and timely account of the incident. You don’t cut corners or expect special treatment for being tired, seeing the thorough report as part of your responsibility. You are reminded of the honor it is to serve in law-enforcement.  
2. You’re exhausted and worried you might make mistakes because of fatigue, so you decide to leave the report for the next morning. Between shifts you consistently think about finishing the report and you worry that you will not remember important details. You plan to arrive early to finish it. All the while you are worried that your supervisor will reprimand you. You have even shared this experience with a trusted friend to assure yourself that what you are doing is OK. This, however, does not reduce your anxiety about not completing it right away. 
3. You realize that although your shift ends soon, if you act quickly, you can finish the report; however, you spend some time thinking about this before you start. You know your supervisor might be upset with a report done hastily, but believe it is the best thing to do because even if the supervisor is upset, it will at least give you time to meet with her.  
4. You choose to complete the report now because you don’t want to inconvenience anyone waiting on it. Despite your fatigue, you put the needs of the department first, reasoning that it’s more considerate to provide the information promptly so others, like investigators or the victim, aren’t adversely affected. 
5. You want to methodically write the full report before ending your shift, double-checking details for accuracy, despite the late hour because that represents the kind of work you consistently do. You like adhering to the rule that paperwork must be done promptly and take pride in finishing the task on time and to the required standard. 
6. You seek a creative solution because there might be one and trying new things has worked well for you before. You suddenly realise that your department-issued tablet has a voice dictation feature, you use it to quickly narrate the report’s details and include the novelty of the situation.

original_sjt.question: It’s mid-afternoon near the end of your shift. After a team response to several calls about an adult Hispanic/Latino subject in emotional distress, your unit successfully ensured the subject’s safety without incident. Now multiple parties—your partners, crisis clinicians, and community outreach officers—depend on accurate records for coordination. Due to department protocol, all reports must be submitted before personnel rotate, and the system requires rapid entry. With paperwork piling up from various officers at once, you notice some peers are rushing their documentation or omitting certain less-noticeable interactions to finish quickly. The policy is clear: submit detailed documentation now. You feel the pressure to keep pace while ensuring everyone on the team gets out promptly.
original_sjt.honesty_humility_option: You insist on entering every interaction and step taken with full honesty, even though you’ll likely be the last one done and will have to explain the delay to your team. Despite seeing others take shortcuts, you focus on precise and comprehensive notes as dictated by department policy, knowing it’s your duty to represent the event faithfully.
original_sjt.emotionality_option: You struggle with worry that hurrying could lead you to make critical mistakes in your notes or let down someone depending on your report; this anxiety makes it hard to start. You ask a colleague for reassurance and support before deciding to methodically log key details now—even if doing so keeps you late and uneasy about peer opinions.
original_sjt.extraversion_option: You quickly discuss documentation strategies with your partners and encourage them to pool information efficiently. Together, you divide tasks for rapid but thorough entries so all necessary facts are included. As a group, you review each other’s notes for any obvious omissions before submitting as a coordinated team.
original_sjt.agreeableness_option: Observing that others might miss their family obligations if they stay late, you willingly accept extra report sections from teammates struggling under the workload. You try to write not just your own notes but help cover gaps for others too, so everyone can get through faster without leaving out crucial information for follow-up services.
original_sjt.conscientiousness_option: You methodically double-check all your entries against established protocol and the scene’s checklist before final submission. You resist peer pressure to rush or cut corners, confident that every step matters for accountability and later reference—knowing you’d rather sacrifice personal time than risk protocol breaches.
original_sjt.openness_option: Noticing delays as others wait their turn at station computers, you improvise by dictating initial findings into your secure mobile device using department-approved apps, drafting structured summaries for yourself and colleagues. honesty_humility.analysis: The option strongly and exclusively demonstrates Honesty-Humility by emphasizing strict adherence to truthful, thorough reporting even at a personal cost, with explicit resistance to shortcuts.

emotionality.analysis: Shows core Emotionality via anxiety and seeking reassurance but mixes some aspects of Conscientiousness (careful record-keeping) and minor Agreeableness (concern about others’ opinions).
emotionality.suggested_correction: Your anxiety about making a mistake with the documentation becomes overwhelming as you recall how errors can seriously affect future care. Rather than rush or hold things up further, you decide to let your supervisor know you're feeling stressed by the situation and ask for advice on handling your report under pressure—prioritizing emotional support over getting ahead quickly.

extraversion.analysis: Option illustrates Extraversion by leading a coordinated, interactive solution through communication and collective action for rapid, accurate results. The focus remains on sociability and teamwork.

agreeableness.analysis: Primarily demonstrates Agreeableness through concern for teammates’ well-being and willingness to take on extra work but slightly bleeds into Conscientiousness (covering info gaps) and Honesty-Humility (self-sacrifice).
agreeableness.suggested_correction: You notice a teammate is falling behind due to workload. Wanting to ease their stress, you volunteer to stay late yourself and take over one simple segment of their reporting—even though you’re tired—so they won’t miss important personal commitments.

conscientiousness.analysis: Portrays high Conscientiousness by strictly following procedure, carefully double-checking entries, and disregarding peer shortcuts, keeping process integrity foremost.

openness.analysis: Captures Openness with technological improvisation and flexibility in approach but somewhat blends into Conscientiousness (ensuring accuracy and deadlines).
openness.suggested_correction: To avoid idle waiting at crowded computers, you adapt by using a new digital reporting feature recently introduced to the department. config.base_scenario:
Question: You’ve just finished handling an assault call near the end of your [time_of_day] shift. You’re very tired, and writing a detailed report now will push your work past the end of shift. No one specifically needs the report until later. You must decide whether to finish the documentation now or later.
Options:

1. You dutifully complete the report right away because it is the most fair thing to do in the current situation. Even if this means staying late to ensure an accurate, honest, and timely account of the incident. You don’t cut corners or expect special treatment for being tired, seeing the thorough report as part of your responsibility. You are reminded of the honor it is to serve in law-enforcement.  
2. You’re exhausted and worried you might make mistakes because of fatigue, so you decide to leave the report for the next morning. Between shifts you consistently think about finishing the report and you worry that you will not remember important details. You plan to arrive early to finish it. All the while you are worried that your supervisor will reprimand you. You have even shared this experience with a trusted friend to assure yourself that what you are doing is OK. This, however, does not reduce your anxiety about not completing it right away. 
3. You realize that although your shift ends soon, if you act quickly, you can finish the report; however, you spend some time thinking about this before you start. You know your supervisor might be upset with a report done hastily, but believe it is the best thing to do because even if the supervisor is upset, it will at least give you time to meet with her.  
4. You choose to complete the report now because you don’t want to inconvenience anyone waiting on it. Despite your fatigue, you put the needs of the department first, reasoning that it’s more considerate to provide the information promptly so others, like investigators or the victim, aren’t adversely affected. 
5. You want to methodically write the full report before ending your shift, double-checking details for accuracy, despite the late hour because that represents the kind of work you consistently do. You like adhering to the rule that paperwork must be done promptly and take pride in finishing the task on time and to the required standard. 
6. You seek a creative solution because there might be one and trying new things has worked well for you before. You suddenly realise that your department-issued tablet has a voice dictation feature, you use it to quickly narrate the report’s details and include the novelty of the situation.

The main subject, a young adult Native American/Alaska Native female, has surrendered peacefully. The procedure is clear and important for agency coordination; however, you notice that others are informally discussing ways to save time on paperwork or leverage recent technology changes to streamline the process. You must decide how to handle completing your required documentation with multiple peers collaborating around you.
original_sjt.honesty_humility_option: You insist on writing a full, transparent account as directed by protocol, even if others use shortcuts. You stay later to ensure accuracy and fairness for everyone involved, declining any special treatment because everyone’s record is equally important.
original_sjt.emotionality_option: You become concerned that the stressful nature of the situation may impact your ability to recall key facts precisely. You consider postponing your report until you feel calmer, asking colleagues for reassurance and sharing your anxieties about possible mistakes in documentation.
original_sjt.extraversion_option: You discuss strategies with teammates before starting, preferring to coordinate details aloud so that no critical perspective is missed. You weigh their opinions before quickly drafting your own report while actively encouraging mutual input from all officers involved.
original_sjt.agreeableness_option: Recognizing how delays might burden administrative staff from different agencies, you choose to promptly complete your portion so nobody else has to wait on you. Even if tired, you focus on easing others' workloads and maintaining inter-agency goodwill.
original_sjt.conscientiousness_option: You follow each step of reporting protocol meticulously, cross-checking details among peers even though some want to move quickly. Upholding the rule that reports must be done precisely and completely regardless of convenience matters most to you.
original_sjt.openness_option: Noting a colleague using digital dictation, you try the new approach as well—combining thoroughness with technology to efficiently document facts. original_sjt.emotionality_option: Noticing the individual's visible anxiety, you approach gently and prioritize reassuring them while collecting information, focusing on their feelings during questioning. You make a point of checking in verbally about their emotional state throughout the interaction and ensure they feel supported despite the circumstances.
original_sjt.extraversion_option: You energetically engage with the subject, using friendly conversation and confident body language to put them at ease. As you gather their account quickly, you use open communication with your supervisor about progress and invite questions from anyone else present to ensure all voices are heard.
original_sjt.agreeableness_option: Wanting to avoid distressing anyone involved, you politely request cooperation from the subject while also assuring them they aren’t in trouble. You go out of your way to be considerate of their situation and are careful not to appear too forceful with directives from your supervisor.
original_sjt.conscientiousness_option: You systematically document each step according to departmental guidelines—even when under time pressure—to ensure accuracy. original_sjt.openness_option: Recognizing both procedural needs and possible barriers for the subject, you suggest conducting part of the statement via secure mobile recording outside the standard protocol, then ask if any cultural factors or language assistance might help clarify their perspective for a fuller picture.

config.base_scenario:
Question: You’ve just finished handling an assault call near the end of your [time_of_day] shift. You’re very tired, and writing a detailed report now will push your work past the end of shift. No one specifically needs the report until later. You must decide whether to finish the documentation now or later.
Options:

1. You dutifully complete the report right away because it is the most fair thing to do in the current situation. Even if this means staying late to ensure an accurate, honest, and timely account of the incident. You don’t cut corners or expect special treatment for being tired, seeing the thorough report as part of your responsibility. You are reminded of the honor it is to serve in law-enforcement.  
2. You’re exhausted and worried you might make mistakes because of fatigue, so you decide to leave the report for the next morning. Between shifts you consistently think about finishing the report and you worry that you will not remember important details. You plan to arrive early to finish it. All the while you are worried that your supervisor will reprimand you. You have even shared this experience with a trusted friend to assure yourself that what you are doing is OK. This, however, does not reduce your anxiety about not completing it right away. 
3. You realize that although your shift ends soon, if you act quickly, you can finish the report; however, you spend some time thinking about this before you start. You know your supervisor might be upset with a report done hastily, but believe it is the best thing to do because even if the supervisor is upset, it will at least give you time to meet with her.  
4. You choose to complete the report now because you don’t want to inconvenience anyone waiting on it. Despite your fatigue, you put the needs of the department first, reasoning that it’s more considerate to provide the information promptly so others, like investigators or the victim, aren’t adversely affected. 
5. You want to methodically write the full report before ending your shift, double-checking details for accuracy, despite the late hour because that represents the kind of work you consistently do. You like adhering to the rule that paperwork must be done promptly and take pride in finishing the task on time and to the required standard. 
6. You seek a creative solution because there might be one and trying new things has worked well for you before. You suddenly realise that your department-issued tablet has a voice dictation feature, you use it to quickly narrate the report’s details and include the novelty of the situation.

original_sjt.question: During a busy afternoon shift, you respond to an emergency call involving a group of teenagers—one, a Hispanic/Latino non-binary juvenile, is suspected of having set off the fire alarm at a local community center. No one was harmed, but building management and several bystanders are upset. There are witnesses, the juvenile’s guardian is present and anxious, your supervisor has requested a thorough account, and everyone is watching how you will handle the situation. Protocol suggests detaining anyone involved, but there is space for discretion regarding juveniles in first-time incidents. How do you decide what to do next?

You refrain from giving special treatment based on emotion or outside pressure, treating every step as part of your duty and ensuring that everyone receives accurate information on outcomes.
original_sjt.emotionality_option: Acknowledging the emotional state of the juvenile and their guardian, you recommend briefly stepping aside with them to hear their concerns and calm them down before deciding next steps. Their distress weighs heavily on your mind, but you still notify your supervisor as expected.
original_sjt.extraversion_option: You engage actively with everyone present—witnesses, guardians, management, and colleagues—seeking input and clarifying facts quickly in front of your supervisor. Your focus is on facilitating clear communication to make sure no perspectives are overlooked before acting.
original_sjt.agreeableness_option: Wanting to be considerate, you mediate between the upset staff and worried guardian, seeking consensus for the fairest way forward. With compassion guiding your approach, you aim to avoid escalating tension by proposing community service as an alternative if everyone agrees.
original_sjt.conscientiousness_option: Following protocol closely, you immediately separate those involved and document statements from each party carefully before reporting everything to your supervisor. Despite pressures from witnesses or management to act swiftly or show leniency, you remain steadfast in observing all required procedures without shortcuts.
original_sjt.openness_option: You consider alternatives within departmental guidelines—such as recommending restorative justice activities or peer-led education instead of detention—presenting these suggestions to your supervisor along with conventional options. agreeableness.suggested_correction: You seek out opinions from both staff and the guardian to find common ground. Remaining diplomatic, you suggest a mutually agreeable solution—such as community service—to resolve the issue constructively.

conscientiousness.analysis: Strict adherence to procedures and resisting external pressure aligns fully with Conscientiousness. The behaviors described are thorough and rule-driven with no significant trait bleed.

openness.analysis: 'Recommending restorative justice' embodies Openness (willingness to innovate), but balancing guidelines and presenting conventional options causes minor bleed into Conscientiousness.
openness.suggested_correction: You proactively suggest novel solutions like restorative justice activities or peer-led workshops instead of detention, focusing on creative ways to achieve positive outcomes while working within permissible boundaries.

Question: You’ve just finished handling an assault call near the end of your [time_of_day] shift. You’re very tired, and writing a detailed report now will push your work past the end of shift. No one specifically needs the report until later. You must decide whether to finish the documentation now or later.
Options:

1. You dutifully complete the report right away because it is the most fair thing to do in the current situation. Even if this means staying late to ensure an accurate, honest, and timely account of the incident. You don’t cut corners or expect special treatment for being tired, seeing the thorough report as part of your responsibility. You are reminded of the honor it is to serve in law-enforcement.  
2. You’re exhausted and worried you might make mistakes because of fatigue, so you decide to leave the report for the next morning. Between shifts you consistently think about finishing the report and you worry that you will not remember important details. You plan to arrive early to finish it. All the while you are worried that your supervisor will reprimand you. You have even shared this experience with a trusted friend to assure yourself that what you are doing is OK. This, however, does not reduce your anxiety about not completing it right away. 
3. You realize that although your shift ends soon, if you act quickly, you can finish the report; however, you spend some time thinking about this before you start. You know your supervisor might be upset with a report done hastily, but believe it is the best thing to do because even if the supervisor is upset, it will at least give you time to meet with her.  
4. You choose to complete the report now because you don’t want to inconvenience anyone waiting on it. Despite your fatigue, you put the needs of the department first, reasoning that it’s more considerate to provide the information promptly so others, like investigators or the victim, aren’t adversely affected. 
5. You want to methodically write the full report before ending your shift, double-checking details for accuracy, despite the late hour because that represents the kind of work you consistently do. You like adhering to the rule that paperwork must be done promptly and take pride in finishing the task on time and to the required standard. 
6. You seek a creative solution because there might be one and trying new things has worked well for you before. You suddenly realise that your department-issued tablet has a voice dictation feature, you use it to quickly narrate the report’s details and include the novelty of the situation.

config.base_scenario:
Question: You’ve just finished handling an assault call near the end of your [time_of_day] shift. You’re very tired, and writing a detailed report now will push your work past the end of shift. No one specifically needs the report until later. You must decide whether to finish the documentation now or later.
Options:

1. You dutifully complete the report right away because it is the most fair thing to do in the current situation. Even if this means staying late to ensure an accurate, honest, and timely account of the incident. You don’t cut corners or expect special treatment for being tired, seeing the thorough report as part of your responsibility. You are reminded of the honor it is to serve in law-enforcement.  
2. You’re exhausted and worried you might make mistakes because of fatigue, so you decide to leave the report for the next morning. Between shifts you consistently think about finishing the report and you worry that you will not remember important details. You plan to arrive early to finish it. All the while you are worried that your supervisor will reprimand you. You have even shared this experience with a trusted friend to assure yourself that what you are doing is OK. This, however, does not reduce your anxiety about not completing it right away. 
3. You realize that although your shift ends soon, if you act quickly, you can finish the report; however, you spend some time thinking about this before you start. You know your supervisor might be upset with a report done hastily, but believe it is the best thing to do because even if the supervisor is upset, it will at least give you time to meet with her.  
4. You choose to complete the report now because you don’t want to inconvenience anyone waiting on it. Despite your fatigue, you put the needs of the department first, reasoning that it’s more considerate to provide the information promptly so others, like investigators or the victim, aren’t adversely affected. 
5. You want to methodically write the full report before ending your shift, double-checking details for accuracy, despite the late hour because that represents the kind of work you consistently do. You like adhering to the rule that paperwork must be done promptly and take pride in finishing the task on time and to the required standard. 
6. You seek a creative solution because there might be one and trying new things has worked well for you before. You suddenly realise that your department-issued tablet has a voice dictation feature, you use it to quickly narrate the report’s details and include the novelty of the situation.

original_sjt.question: It's a quiet afternoon near the end of your shift when you're called to assist with a young adult, described as white, who is showing erratic behavior in the park and possibly struggling emotionally. The person is not aggressive, but seems confused and sits alone. Your supervisor instructs you to check in and write an observation note for department records, but offers no specific direction beyond making contact and using good judgment. Policies around interactions like this have recently changed and you are unsure how strictly to interpret them. You must decide how to proceed, considering both official expectations and the wellbeing of the person.
original_sjt.honesty_humility_option: You approach with openness about your role, calmly introduce yourself to the individual, and communicate clearly that your priority is ensuring their safety without overstepping boundaries. After providing support within your training, you complete the required observation note accurately before leaving for the day, emphasizing in your report where procedures were ambiguous and suggesting improvements for clarity.
original_sjt.emotionality_option: Concerned about potentially overlooking an emotional warning sign, you prioritize your own sense of responsibility by staying with the individual longer than necessary while frequently checking in on them. You write a thorough observation detailing not only their demeanor but also how uneasy you felt given the ambiguous policies and later discuss your concerns privately with your supervisor.
original_sjt.extraversion_option: You engage in active conversation, using a friendly tone to build rapport with the young adult in public view of others at the park. You mention to a passing colleague that you’d like feedback afterwards. For your observation note, you emphasize your efforts at clear communication and summarize input from everyone nearby who briefly engaged during your contact.
original_sjt.agreeableness_option: You focus on empathy, sitting near but respectfully distanced from the young adult to make them feel at ease. Balancing expectations from both the department and the individual's possible discomfort, you note in your report any behaviors suggesting distress and express compassion throughout every action taken so that nobody involved feels disregarded or pushed.
original_sjt.conscientiousness_option: Relying on diligent preparation, you review all recent protocols on interacting with emotionally distressed people before approaching. original_sjt.openness_option: You try a novel approach by offering creative options for support, such as mentioning nearby counseling services or writing resources down for the young adult if they seem receptive.
